sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Allotment money with premium — partial default
questions.question: Sigma Ltd. allotted 50,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2. The amount due on allotment is ₹5 per share, including the premium. The holder of 1,000 shares failed to pay the allotment money. How much allotment money actually reaches the bank?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹2,45,000
Step 1: Shares on which allotment is paid = 50,000 − 1,000 = 49,000
Step 2: Amount received = 49,000 × ₹5 = ₹2,45,000
Common mistake: Assuming full payment gives ₹2,50,000 (A). Leaving out the premium (49,000 × ₹3) gives ₹1,47,000 (C). Deducting only the capital part of the default (₹3,000) gives ₹2,47,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit by one partner, after a salary
questions.question: Alok, Bhumi and Chirag share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Bhumi is entitled to a salary of ₹20,000 a year. Alok personally guarantees Chirag a minimum share of profit of ₹25,000; any deficiency is to be borne by Alok alone. The firm's profit for the year, before Bhumi's salary, is ₹1,40,000. Alok's final share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹55,000
Step 1: Profit after salary = ₹1,40,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Shares 3 : 2 : 1 → Alok ₹60,000; Bhumi ₹40,000; Chirag ₹20,000
Step 3: Chirag's deficiency = ₹25,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹5,000, borne by Alok alone
Step 4: Alok = ₹60,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹55,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives ₹60,000 (B). Sharing the deficiency 3 : 2 with Bhumi gives ₹57,000 (C). Forgetting Bhumi's salary gives ₹68,333 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — Profit and Loss Suspense Account
questions.question: On the death of a partner during the year, his share of profit up to the date of death is credited to his Capital Account and debited to:
options: A) Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
B) Profit and Loss Suspense Account
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Profit and Loss Suspense Account
Why: The firm's accounts are not closed on the date of death, so the estimated share is debited to a temporary P&L Suspense Account, which is closed when the year's profit is known.
Why not the others:
(A) The year's Appropriation Account is not yet prepared.
(C) Revaluation deals with assets and liabilities.
(D) The Executor's Account is CREDITED with the final amount due.
Key point: Mid-year share of profit → P&L Suspense A/c Dr.; To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture after allotment is paid but call is not
questions.question: Ritika held 300 shares of ₹10 each, issued at par and payable ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment and ₹3 on the first and final call. She paid the application and allotment money but not the call, and her shares were forfeited. The amount credited to the Share Forfeiture Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,100
Step 1: Amount paid per share = ₹3 + ₹4 = ₹7
Step 2: Forfeiture = 300 × ₹7 = ₹2,100 (Share Capital Dr. ₹3,000; To Share First and Final Call ₹900; To Share Forfeiture ₹2,100)
Common mistake: ₹3,000 (A) is the called-up capital. ₹900 (B) is the unpaid call. ₹1,200 (D) is only the allotment money.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — rejection plus pro-rata, cash on allotment
questions.question: Comet Ltd. offered 15,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹1. It received applications for 30,000 shares. Applications for 6,000 shares were rejected and their money refunded; the remaining applicants were allotted the 15,000 shares pro rata. Application money was ₹3 per share and allotment money ₹4 per share (including the premium); excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. Assuming all money due was received, the cash received on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹33,000
Step 1: Applications considered for allotment = 30,000 − 6,000 = 24,000 shares
Step 2: Excess application money = (24,000 − 15,000) × ₹3 = ₹27,000, adjusted towards allotment
Step 3: Allotment due = 15,000 × ₹4 = ₹60,000
Step 4: Cash received = ₹60,000 − ₹27,000 = ₹33,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the adjustment gives ₹60,000 (A). Ignoring the rejection (excess ₹45,000) gives ₹15,000 (B). Deducting the refunded amount (6,000 × ₹3) instead gives ₹42,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — average profit adjusted for partners' remuneration
questions.question: A firm's average profit is ₹1,00,000. This is calculated before any remuneration to the partners; a fair remuneration for their services would be ₹20,000 a year in total. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,60,000
Step 1: Adjusted average profit = ₹1,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹80,000 (partners' services have a cost that the profit must bear)
Step 2: Goodwill = ₹80,000 × 2 = ₹1,60,000
Common mistake: Not adjusting gives ₹2,00,000 (A). Adding the remuneration instead of deducting it gives ₹1,20,000 for one year (B). Taking only one year's purchase gives ₹80,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Types of preference shares
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of preference share)
(A) Cumulative
(B) Participating
(C) Convertible
(D) Redeemable

List-II (Feature)
(I) Unpaid dividend of any year is carried forward and paid later
(II) Shares in surplus profits after equity dividend
(III) Can be converted into equity shares
(IV) Repaid by the company after a fixed period
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Cumulative → arrears of dividend accumulate (I).
(B) Participating → extra share in surplus profit (II).
(C) Convertible → may become equity shares (III).
(D) Redeemable → returned after a period (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps cumulative and participating; (B) swaps participating and convertible; (D) swaps cumulative and redeemable.
Key point: Each type adds one special right to the basic preference.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Methods of valuing goodwill — formulas
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Method)
(A) Average profit method
(B) Super profit method
(C) Capitalisation of average profit
(D) Capitalisation of super profit

List-II (Goodwill)
(I) Average profit × Number of years' purchase
(II) (Average profit − Normal profit) × Number of years' purchase
(III) (Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate) − Capital employed
(IV) Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Average profit is multiplied by the years' purchase (I).
(B) Only the super profit is multiplied (II).
(C) The capitalised value of average profit less capital employed (III).
(D) The super profit capitalised at the normal rate (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the average and super profit methods; (B) swaps super profit and capitalisation of average profit; (C) swaps the two methods that use years' purchase and capitalisation.
Key point: 'Years' purchase' methods multiply; 'capitalisation' methods divide by the normal rate.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital treated as a charge
questions.question:
Assertion (A): If the partnership deed treats interest on capital as a charge against profit, it is allowed even when the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): A charge against profit must be provided whether the firm earns a profit or incurs a loss.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Normally, interest on capital is an appropriation and is allowed only out of profits. When the deed makes it a CHARGE, it is debited to the P&L Account like an expense and must be allowed even in a loss year — exactly because charges do not depend on profit (R).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: The deed decides whether interest on capital is a charge or an appropriation.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — refund of surplus after adjusting allotment
questions.question: Nimbus Ltd. received applications for 40,000 shares against 10,000 shares offered and allotted pro rata to all applicants. Application money was ₹4 per share and allotment money ₹3 per share. Excess application money was first adjusted against allotment and any surplus was refunded. The amount refunded is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹90,000
Step 1: Application money received = 40,000 × ₹4 = ₹1,60,000; needed for 10,000 shares = ₹40,000 → excess ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Allotment due = 10,000 × ₹3 = ₹30,000, fully covered by the excess
Step 3: Refund = ₹1,20,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹90,000
Common mistake: Refunding the whole excess gives ₹1,20,000 (B). ₹30,000 (C) is the amount adjusted. ₹60,000 (D) has no basis.
Key point: Excess is adjusted against allotment (and calls, if the terms allow) — only the balance is refunded.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Section 48 — first payment out of realised assets
questions.question: Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the amounts realised from the assets of a dissolved firm are FIRST used to pay:
options: C) The debts of the firm to third parties
D) The partners' current account balances
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The debts of the firm to third parties
Why: Section 48 sets the order: first debts to outsiders, then each partner's loans and advances, then each partner's capital, and finally any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) rank AFTER outside creditors.
Key point: Outsiders → partners' loans → capitals → surplus.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final payment to a partner with a loan and an asset taken over
questions.question: On dissolution, partner Arya has a capital of ₹40,000 and has also lent ₹10,000 to the firm. Her share of the profit on realisation is ₹4,000, and she took over furniture at ₹6,000. The total cash paid to Arya (for her loan and her capital) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹48,000
Step 1: Loan repaid = ₹10,000 (paid before capitals)
Step 2: Capital: ₹40,000 + ₹4,000 (profit) − ₹6,000 (furniture) = ₹38,000
Step 3: Total cash = ₹10,000 + ₹38,000 = ₹48,000
Common mistake: Leaving out the loan gives ₹38,000 (B). Not deducting the furniture gives ₹54,000 (C). Adding the furniture instead gives ₹60,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on debentures — tax deducted at source
questions.question: A company has issued 10% debentures of ₹4,00,000, with interest payable half-yearly. Tax is deducted at source at 10% on the interest. The net amount paid to debenture holders each half-year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹18,000
Step 1: Half-yearly interest = ₹4,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹20,000
Step 2: TDS at 10% = ₹2,000 (credited to TDS Payable and deposited with the government)
Step 3: Net paid = ₹20,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹18,000
Common mistake: ₹20,000 (A) is the gross interest. ₹40,000 (B) is the annual gross interest. ₹36,000 (C) is the annual net payment.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares — order of events
questions.question:
Arrange the following stages of a public issue of shares in the correct order:
(A) Allotment of shares
(B) Receipt of applications with application money
(C) Issue of the prospectus
(D) Making calls on the shares
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (A), (D)
Why: The company invites the public through a prospectus (C); the public applies with application money (B); the directors allot shares (A); the remaining amounts are collected through calls (D).
Why not the others: (A) applications cannot come before the prospectus. (B) allotment cannot come before applications. (D) begins with allotment.
Key point: Prospectus → application → allotment → calls.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account — contents
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account of a firm:
(A) It is an extension of the Profit and Loss Account.
(B) Interest on drawings is credited to it.
(C) A transfer to General Reserve is debited to it.
(D) Rent paid to a partner for the use of his building is debited to it.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The Appropriation Account starts with the net profit from the P&L Account and shows how it is distributed (A). Interest on drawings adds to the profit available (B), while a transfer to reserve is an appropriation (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — rent to a partner is a CHARGE against profit, debited to the P&L Account, not an appropriation. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Expenses → P&L A/c; distribution of profit → Appropriation A/c.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — options available to directors
questions.question:
When an issue of shares is over-subscribed, the directors may:
(A) Reject some applications in full and refund their money.
(B) Allot shares to all applicants on a pro-rata basis.
(C) Use a combination of full rejection and pro-rata allotment.
(D) Allot more shares than were offered in the prospectus.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The directors may reject some applications outright (A), allot proportionately to everyone (B), or combine both methods (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the company can allot only the number of shares offered; it cannot allot more than the issue. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Over-subscription → reject, pro-rata, or both — never over-allot.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Distribution of a loss — interest on drawings, no interest on capital
questions.question: Gopal and Hari share profits and losses in the ratio 2 : 1. The firm's net LOSS for the year, as per the Profit and Loss Account, is ₹18,000. The deed provides interest on capital at 10% p.a. (as an appropriation) on capitals of ₹1,00,000 and ₹50,000, and interest on drawings of ₹1,200 for Gopal and ₹600 for Hari. Gopal's share of the loss is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹10,800
Step 1: Interest on capital is an appropriation, so it is NOT allowed in a loss year
Step 2: Interest on drawings (₹1,800) is still charged and reduces the loss: ₹18,000 − ₹1,800 = ₹16,200
Step 3: Gopal's share = ₹16,200 × 2/3 = ₹10,800
Common mistake: Ignoring interest on drawings gives ₹12,000 (A). Allowing interest on capital (loss ₹31,200) gives ₹20,800 (C). Sharing equally gives ₹8,100 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — what is and is not transferred
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Realisation Account:
(A) The provision for doubtful debts is transferred to its credit side.
(B) A partner's loan to the firm is not transferred to it.
(C) Cash and bank balances are not transferred to it.
(D) General Reserve is transferred to its credit side.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Provisions against assets go to the credit side along with the liabilities (A). Partners' loans are settled directly (B). Cash and bank are the means of settlement, so they remain outside (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — accumulated profits such as General Reserve are credited directly to the partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Realisation A/c = assets, outside liabilities and their provisions only.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — preference shares
questions.question: Shares that carry a preferential right to dividend and to the return of capital on winding up are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Preference shares
Why: Under Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013, preference shares carry both preferential rights — dividend before equity shareholders, and repayment of capital first on winding up.
Why not the others:
(B) Equity shares carry the residual risk.
(C) Sweat equity shares are given for know-how or services.
(D) Bonus shares are issued free out of reserves.
Key point: Preference = priority in dividend + priority in capital repayment.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the retirement of a partner:
(A) The balance of the retiring partner's Capital Account may be transferred to his Loan Account.
(B) Gaining ratio = New ratio − Old ratio.
(C) The continuing partners may agree on any new profit-sharing ratio between themselves.
(D) The retiring partner's share of goodwill must always be credited to a Goodwill Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: An unpaid balance becomes a loan (A). Each continuing partner's gain is new share minus old share (B). The continuing partners are free to fix their future ratio (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — under current practice, goodwill is NOT raised in the books; the retiring partner's share is adjusted through the Capital Accounts of the gaining partners. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Goodwill on retirement → Gaining Partners' Capital Dr.; To Retiring Partner's Capital.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Unrecorded liability paid on dissolution
questions.question: On dissolution, an unrecorded liability of ₹5,000 for outstanding repairs had to be paid in cash. The entry is:
options: A) Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
B) Repairs A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
C) Cash A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Realisation A/c ₹5,000
D) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
Why: The liability was not in the books, so it was never credited to the Realisation Account. Paying it is a loss on realisation, debited to the Realisation Account.
Why not the others:
(A) Capitals are affected only through the realisation result.
(B) Nominal expense accounts are not used on dissolution.
(C) records a receipt, not a payment.
Key point: Unrecorded liability paid → Realisation Dr.; To Cash.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on a partner's loan given during the year (deed silent)
questions.question: Zoya lent ₹50,000 to her firm on 1 October 2025. The partnership deed says nothing about interest on partners' loans, and the books close on 31 March 2026. The interest on her loan for 2025-26 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,500
Step 1: Deed silent → interest on a partner's loan at 6% p.a. (Section 13(d))
Step 2: Period = 1 October to 31 March = 6 months
Step 3: Interest = ₹50,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,500 — a charge against profit, credited to her Loan Account
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹3,000 (A). Using 12% for a full year gives ₹6,000 (B). Using 10% for 6 months gives ₹2,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Sacrificing ratio when only one partner sacrifices
questions.question: Ashok and Basu share profits in the ratio 5 : 3. They admit Chandan, and the new profit-sharing ratio of Ashok, Basu and Chandan is 4 : 3 : 1. Who gives up a share of profit for Chandan, and in what ratio?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Only Ashok sacrifices (1 : 0)
Step 1: Ashok = 5/8 − 4/8 = 1/8 (sacrifice)
Step 2: Basu = 3/8 − 3/8 = 0 (no change)
Step 3: So Chandan's whole share (1/8) comes from Ashok; any premium for goodwill goes to Ashok alone
Common mistake: Assuming the old ratio gives 5 : 3 (A). 4 : 3 (B) is part of the new ratio. 1 : 1 (D) assumes equal sacrifice.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation loss with provision, investment fluctuation reserve and expenses
questions.question: On dissolution, the balance sheet shows: debtors ₹30,000 with a provision for doubtful debts of ₹2,000; stock ₹40,000; investments ₹20,000 with an Investment Fluctuation Reserve of ₹3,000; creditors ₹25,000; and bills payable ₹5,000. Debtors realised ₹27,000; partner Bindu took over the stock at ₹36,000; investments were sold for ₹18,000; creditors were paid ₹24,000 and bills payable in full; and realisation expenses were ₹1,500. The Investment Fluctuation Reserve is distributed directly to the partners. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹7,500
Step 1: Debit side = debtors 30,000 + stock 40,000 + investments 20,000 + creditors paid 24,000 + bills payable paid 5,000 + expenses 1,500 = ₹1,20,500
Step 2: Credit side = provision 2,000 + creditors 25,000 + bills payable 5,000 + debtors realised 27,000 + stock taken by Bindu 36,000 + investments sold 18,000 = ₹1,13,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹1,20,500 − ₹1,13,000 = ₹7,500
Common mistake: Crediting the reserve to the Realisation Account gives ₹4,500 (A). Forgetting the provision gives ₹9,500 (B). Forgetting the expenses gives ₹6,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Features of partnership — mutual agency
questions.question: Every partner is both an agent of the firm and a principal for the acts of the other partners in the course of business. This feature of partnership is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mutual agency
Why: The business may be carried on by all the partners or by any of them acting for all. Each partner therefore binds the others (as their agent) and is bound by them (as a principal).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are features of a COMPANY. Partners' liability is unlimited, and a firm has no separate legal entity or perpetual succession.
Key point: Mutual agency is the true test of a partnership.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — General Reserve
questions.question: At the time of a partner's retirement, the General Reserve appearing in the balance sheet is distributed among:
options: A) The continuing partners in their new ratio
C) All the partners in their old ratio
D) The continuing partners in their gaining ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) All the partners in their old ratio
Why: The reserve was built from past profits, which all partners (including the retiring one) earned in the old ratio. Entry: General Reserve A/c Dr.; To All Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio).
Why not the others: (A) and (D) would deny the retiring partner his share. (B) would deny the others theirs.
Key point: Past profits and losses → all partners, old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Salary and commission on profit after charging both
questions.question: Ankit and Bhavya share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. Ankit gets a salary of ₹12,000 a year. Bhavya gets a commission of 10% of the net profit after charging both Ankit's salary and her own commission. The profit before these items is ₹1,22,000. The total amount credited to Ankit (salary plus share of profit) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹72,000
Step 1: Profit after salary = ₹1,22,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹1,10,000
Step 2: Bhavya's commission = ₹1,10,000 × 10/110 = ₹10,000
Step 3: Divisible profit = ₹1,00,000 → Ankit's share (3/5) = ₹60,000
Step 4: Ankit's total = ₹12,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹72,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the commission gives ₹78,000 (B). Taking 10% of ₹1,10,000 (₹11,000) gives ₹71,400 (C). ₹60,000 (D) leaves out the salary.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Purchase of a business for less than net assets, paid in shares at a premium
questions.question: Ocean Ltd. took over assets of ₹5,00,000 and liabilities of ₹1,00,000 of Marine Traders for ₹3,60,000, paid by issuing equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 20%. The number of shares issued, and the capital profit or goodwill recorded, are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 30,000 shares; Capital Reserve ₹40,000
Step 1: Net assets = ₹5,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000; consideration ₹3,60,000 is less → Capital Reserve ₹40,000
Step 2: Issue price = ₹10 + 20% = ₹12 → shares = ₹3,60,000 ÷ ₹12 = 30,000
Common mistake: Dividing by the face value gives 36,000 shares — (B) and (D). Treating the difference as goodwill gives (C) and (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares — working back the number re-issued
questions.question: A company forfeited 400 shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, on which ₹6 per share had been paid. Some of these shares were re-issued at ₹7 per share as fully paid, and ₹900 was then transferred to Capital Reserve. The number of shares re-issued is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 300
Step 1: Forfeited amount per share = ₹6
Step 2: Discount on re-issue per share = ₹10 − ₹7 = ₹3
Step 3: Capital Reserve per share re-issued = ₹6 − ₹3 = ₹3
Step 4: Shares re-issued = ₹900 ÷ ₹3 = 300
Common mistake: Assuming all were re-issued gives 400 (A). Dividing by ₹6 gives 150 (B). Dividing by ₹4 (the unpaid amount) gives 225 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in advance — presentation
questions.question: In a company's balance sheet, calls received in advance are shown under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Other current liabilities
Why: Money received before a call is made is not yet share capital. The company owes it back to the shareholder until the call is made (and may pay interest on it), so it is a current liability.
Why not the others:
(A) It becomes capital only when the call is made.
(C) It is not a profit or reserve.
(D) It is a definite amount, not a provision.
Key point: Calls in advance → other current liabilities (with any interest accrued on them).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — existing goodwill written off and premium received
questions.question: Ayan and Bina share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. Their balance sheet shows Goodwill of ₹30,000. Chirag is admitted for a 1/5th share and brings ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill in cash; Ayan and Bina sacrifice in their old ratio. The existing goodwill is written off. The net effect of these two goodwill transactions on Ayan's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Debit of ₹6,000
Step 1: Existing goodwill written off in the old ratio → Ayan debited 3/5 × ₹30,000 = ₹18,000
Step 2: Premium shared in the sacrificing ratio (3 : 2) → Ayan credited 3/5 × ₹20,000 = ₹12,000
Step 3: Net = −₹18,000 + ₹12,000 = −₹6,000 → debit
Common mistake: Considering only the premium gives (B). Considering only the write-off gives (C). Reversing the sign gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — capital withdrawn during the year
questions.question: Yash's capital on 1 April 2025 was ₹3,00,000. On 1 January 2026 he withdrew ₹60,000 from his capital. Interest on capital is allowed at 8% p.a., and the books close on 31 March 2026. His interest on capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹22,800
Step 1: Interest on ₹3,00,000 for 9 months (1 April–31 December) = ₹3,00,000 × 8% × 9/12 = ₹18,000
Step 2: Interest on ₹2,40,000 for 3 months (1 January–31 March) = ₹2,40,000 × 8% × 3/12 = ₹4,800
Step 3: Total = ₹22,800
Common mistake: Ignoring the withdrawal gives ₹24,000 (A). Using the reduced capital for the whole year gives ₹19,200 (C). Treating the withdrawal as outstanding for 6 months gives ₹21,600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation — unrecorded items and depreciation
questions.question: On reconstitution, the following are found: unrecorded investments worth ₹6,000; an unrecorded outstanding salary of ₹4,000; machinery of ₹50,000 to be depreciated by 10%; and prepaid insurance of ₹1,500 not shown in the books. The result of revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Loss of ₹1,500
Step 1: Gains — unrecorded investments +₹6,000; prepaid insurance +₹1,500
Step 2: Losses — outstanding salary −₹4,000; depreciation on machinery −₹5,000
Step 3: Net = 7,500 − 9,000 = −₹1,500 → loss
Common mistake: Reversing the sign gives (A). Ignoring the unrecorded investments gives a loss of ₹7,500 (C). Treating every item as a gain gives ₹16,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Workmen Compensation Reserve — excess over the claim
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On admission, the excess of the Workmen Compensation Reserve over the actual claim is credited to the old partners in their old ratio.
Reason (R): The excess reserve is an accumulated profit that belongs to the old partners.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Once the claim is provided for, the unused part of the reserve is simply past profit set aside earlier. Past profits belong to the old partners (R), so the excess is credited to them in the old ratio (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Reserve − claim → old partners; claim − reserve → Revaluation A/c.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Return on debentures
questions.question: The fixed return that a company pays to its debenture holders is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Interest
Why: Debenture holders are lenders, so their return is interest at a fixed rate, payable whether or not the company makes a profit.
Why not the others:
(A) Dividend is paid to shareholders out of profits.
(C) A premium may be paid on redemption, but it is not the regular return.
(D) Bonus refers to free shares.
Key point: Debentures → interest; shares → dividend.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — retiring partner's share of goodwill
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Mehta, Nanda and Oberoi are partners sharing profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Oberoi retires on 31 March 2026. On that date, Oberoi's capital is ₹60,000; the balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹25,000; and the revaluation of assets and liabilities shows a profit of ₹15,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,10,000; it is not to appear in the books and is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts. Mehta and Nanda will share future profits equally. The total amount due to Oberoi is transferred to his Loan Account, to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the unpaid balance. The first instalment falls due on 31 March 2027.

Question: How much is Oberoi entitled to receive for his share of goodwill?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹22,000
Step 1: Oberoi's share = 1/5
Step 2: ₹1,10,000 × 1/5 = ₹22,000
Common mistake: ₹1,10,000 (A) is the firm's goodwill. ₹44,000 (C) is the share of Mehta or Nanda (2/5). ₹11,000 (D) is the amount each continuing partner pays.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — amount transferred to the loan account
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Mehta, Nanda and Oberoi are partners sharing profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Oberoi retires on 31 March 2026. On that date, Oberoi's capital is ₹60,000; the balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹25,000; and the revaluation of assets and liabilities shows a profit of ₹15,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,10,000; it is not to appear in the books and is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts. Mehta and Nanda will share future profits equally. The total amount due to Oberoi is transferred to his Loan Account, to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the unpaid balance. The first instalment falls due on 31 March 2027.

Question: Once every adjustment has been made, what balance moves from Oberoi's Capital Account into his Loan Account?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹90,000
Step 1: Capital ₹60,000
Step 2: Add share of General Reserve (1/5 × ₹25,000) = ₹5,000
Step 3: Add share of revaluation profit (1/5 × ₹15,000) = ₹3,000
Step 4: Add share of goodwill = ₹22,000
Step 5: Total = ₹90,000
Common mistake: Ignoring goodwill gives ₹68,000 (A). Ignoring the reserve and revaluation gives ₹82,000 (B). Ignoring the revaluation profit gives ₹87,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — continuing partner's goodwill contribution
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Mehta, Nanda and Oberoi are partners sharing profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Oberoi retires on 31 March 2026. On that date, Oberoi's capital is ₹60,000; the balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹25,000; and the revaluation of assets and liabilities shows a profit of ₹15,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,10,000; it is not to appear in the books and is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts. Mehta and Nanda will share future profits equally. The total amount due to Oberoi is transferred to his Loan Account, to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the unpaid balance. The first instalment falls due on 31 March 2027.

Question: The amount debited to Mehta's Capital Account for Oberoi's share of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹11,000
Step 1: Gains: Mehta = 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10; Nanda = 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10 → gaining ratio 1 : 1
Step 2: Mehta's debit = ₹22,000 × 1/2 = ₹11,000
Common mistake: Charging Mehta with all of it gives ₹22,000 (B). Using 2/5 of ₹22,000 gives ₹8,800 (C). ₹44,000 (D) is Mehta's share of the firm's goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retiring partner's loan — first instalment with interest
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Mehta, Nanda and Oberoi are partners sharing profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Oberoi retires on 31 March 2026. On that date, Oberoi's capital is ₹60,000; the balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹25,000; and the revaluation of assets and liabilities shows a profit of ₹15,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,10,000; it is not to appear in the books and is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts. Mehta and Nanda will share future profits equally. The total amount due to Oberoi is transferred to his Loan Account, to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the unpaid balance. The first instalment falls due on 31 March 2027.

Question: The total amount paid to Oberoi on 31 March 2027 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹39,000
Step 1: Principal instalment = ₹90,000 ÷ 3 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Interest for 2026-27 on the full unpaid balance = ₹90,000 × 10% = ₹9,000
Step 3: Payment = ₹30,000 + ₹9,000 = ₹39,000
Common mistake: Leaving out interest gives ₹30,000 (A). ₹36,000 (B) is the SECOND payment (₹30,000 + 10% of ₹60,000). Charging interest on the instalment only gives ₹33,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retiring partner's loan — total interest over the repayment period
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Mehta, Nanda and Oberoi are partners sharing profits in the ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Oberoi retires on 31 March 2026. On that date, Oberoi's capital is ₹60,000; the balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹25,000; and the revaluation of assets and liabilities shows a profit of ₹15,000. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,10,000; it is not to appear in the books and is adjusted through the partners' Capital Accounts. Mehta and Nanda will share future profits equally. The total amount due to Oberoi is transferred to his Loan Account, to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the unpaid balance. The first instalment falls due on 31 March 2027.

Question: The total interest paid to Oberoi over the three years is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹18,000
Step 1: Year 1 — on ₹90,000 = ₹9,000
Step 2: Year 2 — on ₹60,000 = ₹6,000
Step 3: Year 3 — on ₹30,000 = ₹3,000
Step 4: Total = ₹18,000
Common mistake: Charging ₹9,000 every year gives ₹27,000 (A). ₹9,000 (C) is only the first year. Leaving out the final year gives ₹15,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — average payment period in days
questions.question: Net credit purchases for the year (365 days) are ₹7,30,000 and average trade payables are ₹1,00,000. The average payment period is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 50 days
Step 1: Trade payables turnover = ₹7,30,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 7.3 times
Step 2: Average payment period = 365 ÷ 7.3 = 50 days
Common mistake: 7.3 (A) is the turnover ratio, not days. 73 days (B) misplaces the decimal. 60 days (D) uses 360 days and rounds wrongly.
Key point: A shorter payment period means suppliers are paid faster.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Operating ratio — net profit including non-operating items
questions.question: A company's revenue from operations is ₹5,00,000 and its operating ratio is 85%. It also has non-operating income of ₹10,000 and non-operating expenses of ₹4,000. Its net profit (before tax) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹81,000
Step 1: Operating cost = 85% × ₹5,00,000 = ₹4,25,000 → operating profit = ₹75,000
Step 2: Net profit = ₹75,000 + ₹10,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹81,000
Common mistake: ₹75,000 (B) is the operating profit only. Adding both non-operating items gives ₹89,000 (C). Reversing them gives ₹69,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from financing activities — borrowings, interest and dividend
questions.question: During the year, a trading company raised long-term borrowings of ₹2,00,000, repaid a bank loan of ₹50,000, paid interest of ₹18,000 on loans and paid a dividend of ₹12,000. Net cash flow from financing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,20,000 inflow
Step 1: Inflow — borrowings ₹2,00,000
Step 2: Outflows — repayment ₹50,000; interest ₹18,000; dividend ₹12,000
Step 3: Net = 2,00,000 − 50,000 − 18,000 − 12,000 = ₹1,20,000 inflow
Common mistake: Ignoring interest and dividend gives ₹1,50,000 (B). Ignoring the dividend gives ₹1,32,000 (C). Ignoring the interest gives ₹1,38,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — income tax paid from the provision account
questions.question: Cash generated from operations is ₹2,40,000. The Provision for Tax account shows an opening balance of ₹30,000 and a closing balance of ₹45,000, and ₹50,000 was provided for tax during the year. Net cash from operating activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,05,000
Step 1: Tax paid = Opening provision + Provided during the year − Closing provision = 30,000 + 50,000 − 45,000 = ₹35,000
Step 2: Net cash from operating activities = ₹2,40,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹2,05,000
Common mistake: Deducting the provision made (₹50,000) gives ₹1,90,000 (A). Deducting only the change in the provision (₹15,000) gives ₹2,25,000 (B). Ignoring tax gives ₹2,40,000 (D).
Key point: Only tax actually PAID is a cash outflow.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Limitations of ratio analysis
questions.question:
Which of the following are limitations of accounting ratios?
(A) They are based on historical data.
(B) They ignore qualitative factors such as the quality of management.
(C) Different accounting policies reduce their comparability between firms.
(D) Ratios alone are enough to reach a final conclusion about a business.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Ratios use past figures (A), capture only what is measured in money (B), and can mislead when firms use different methods, such as of depreciation or inventory valuation (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is not a limitation — it is a misconception. Ratios are only indicators and must be read with other information. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Ratios are tools for judgement, not substitutes for it.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Inventory turnover — working back to opening inventory
questions.question: A firm's inventory turnover ratio is 5 times and its cost of revenue from operations is ₹4,00,000. Closing inventory is ₹20,000 more than opening inventory. Opening inventory is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹70,000
Step 1: Average inventory = ₹4,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Opening + Closing = ₹1,60,000, and Closing = Opening + ₹20,000
Step 3: 2 × Opening + ₹20,000 = ₹1,60,000 → Opening = ₹70,000 (Closing = ₹90,000)
Common mistake: ₹80,000 (A) is the average inventory. ₹90,000 (B) is the closing inventory. ₹60,000 (C) subtracts the ₹20,000 from the average.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of analysis — common-size statements
questions.question: Which tool of financial analysis expresses every item as a percentage of a common base, such as revenue from operations or total assets?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Common-size statements
Why: Common-size statements (vertical analysis) show each item as a percentage of a base — revenue in the income statement, total assets or total liabilities in the balance sheet.
Why not the others:
(A) Comparative statements show changes between years.
(C) Trend analysis uses a base year index.
(D) The cash flow statement shows cash movements.
Key point: Common base = vertical analysis.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Current ratio — working back from a change
questions.question: A company's current ratio is 2 : 1. After it pays creditors ₹30,000 in cash, the current ratio rises to 2.5 : 1. Its current assets BEFORE the payment were:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,80,000
Step 1: Let current liabilities = L; current assets = 2L
Step 2: After payment: (2L − 30,000) ÷ (L − 30,000) = 2.5
Step 3: 2L − 30,000 = 2.5L − 75,000 → 0.5L = 45,000 → L = ₹90,000
Step 4: Current assets = 2 × ₹90,000 = ₹1,80,000 (after payment ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹60,000 = 2.5 ✔)
Common mistake: ₹90,000 (A) is the current liabilities. ₹1,50,000 (B) is current assets AFTER the payment. ₹60,000 (C) is current liabilities after the payment.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — purchased goodwill
questions.question: Goodwill purchased by a company is shown in its balance sheet under:
options: A) Non-current assets — Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets (Intangible assets)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Non-current assets — Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets (Intangible assets)
Why: Purchased goodwill is a long-term intangible asset, so Schedule III places it under Intangible assets, within the PPE and Intangible Assets heading.
Why not the others:
(B) Investments are holdings in other entities.
(C) Other non-current assets include items such as long-term trade receivables.
(D) Reserves are part of equity, not assets.
Key point: Goodwill, patents, trademarks, software → Intangible assets.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Classification of ratios
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Current ratio
(B) Interest coverage ratio
(C) Trade receivables turnover ratio
(D) Operating profit ratio

List-II (Category)
(I) Liquidity ratio
(II) Solvency ratio
(III) Activity (turnover) ratio
(IV) Profitability ratio
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) The current ratio measures short-term paying ability (I).
(B) Interest coverage measures the long-term ability to service debt (II).
(C) Receivables turnover measures how quickly debtors pay (III).
(D) Operating profit ratio measures earnings on revenue (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps liquidity and solvency; (C) swaps solvency and activity; (D) swaps liquidity and profitability.
Key point: Four families — liquidity, solvency, activity, profitability.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — ROUNDUP
questions.question: The formula =ROUNDUP(1234.561,1) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1234.6
Why: ROUNDUP always rounds away from zero to the given number of digits. To 1 decimal place, 1234.561 becomes 1234.6.
Why not the others:
(A) 1234.5 is ROUNDDOWN to 1 decimal.
(C) 1235 is rounding to 0 decimals.
(D) 1240 is rounding to −1 digits (tens).
Key point: ROUNDUP never decreases a positive number.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — MAX and MIN
questions.question: Cells B2 to B5 of a salary sheet contain 18,000; 25,000; 22,500 and 30,000. To find the spread between the highest and lowest salary, the accountant enters =MAX(B2:B5)-MIN(B2:B5). The result is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 12,000
Step 1: MAX = 30,000; MIN = 18,000
Step 2: Difference = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000 (the range of salaries)
Common mistake: 30,000 (A) is the MAX alone. 18,000 (B) is the MIN alone. 95,500 (C) is the SUM.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — range notation
questions.question: The block of cells from A1 to C5 is written in a spreadsheet formula as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A1:C5
Why: A colon joins the first and last cells of a range, so A1:C5 covers 3 columns × 5 rows = 15 cells, as in =SUM(A1:C5).
Why not the others:
(A) A hyphen is subtraction.
(B) A semicolon is not a range operator.
(C) & joins text.
Key point: Colon (:) = range.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — overtime with an IF formula
questions.question: A payroll sheet pays double the hourly rate for every hour worked beyond 200 in a month: =IF(D2>200,(D2-200)*E2*2,0). An employee worked 230 hours (D2) at an hourly rate of ₹150 (E2). The overtime pay calculated is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹9,000
Step 1: Test: 230 > 200 is TRUE, so the first expression is used
Step 2: Extra hours = 230 − 200 = 30
Step 3: Overtime = 30 × ₹150 × 2 = ₹9,000
Common mistake: Forgetting the double rate gives ₹4,500 (A). Doubling all 230 hours gives ₹69,000 (B). Reading the condition as false gives 0 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — VLOOKUP with exact match
questions.question:
An employee master table occupies A2:C5:
Row 2: E101 | Sales | 28,000
Row 3: E102 | Purchase | 30,500
Row 4: E103 | Accounts | 32,000
Row 5: E104 | HR | 26,000
The formula =VLOOKUP("E103",A2:C5,3,FALSE) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 32,000
Step 1: VLOOKUP searches the FIRST column (A2:A5) for 'E103' and finds it in row 4
Step 2: Column index 3 → it returns the third column of that row: 32,000
Step 3: FALSE requires an exact match, which exists
Common mistake: 'Accounts' (B) is column 2. #N/A (C) appears only when no exact match exists. 'E103' (D) is column 1.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — SUMIF for an expense category
questions.question: In an expense sheet, cells B2:B6 contain the heads Rent, Salary, Rent, Electricity and Rent, and cells C2:C6 contain the amounts 5,000; 20,000; 5,000; 1,200 and 5,500. The formula =SUMIF(B2:B6,"Rent",C2:C6) returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 15,500
Why: SUMIF adds the amounts in C2:C6 only where the matching cell in B2:B6 equals 'Rent': 5,000 + 5,000 + 5,500 = 15,500.
Why not the others:
(A) 10,000 misses the third Rent entry.
(B) 36,700 is the total of all expenses.
(D) 3 is what COUNTIF would return.
Key point: SUMIF(criteria range, criterion, sum range).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — sorting
questions.question: To arrange a list of debtors in descending order of amount due, the spreadsheet feature to use is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Sort
Why: Sort rearranges rows in ascending or descending order of a chosen column, such as the amount due.
Why not the others:
(A) Filter hides the rows that do not meet a condition, without reordering them.
(C) Data Validation controls input.
(D) Merge joins cells for formatting.
Key point: Sort = reorder; Filter = show selected rows.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — net salary with employee's PF
questions.question: An employee's basic pay is ₹25,000, DA is 20% of basic, and conveyance allowance is ₹1,600. The employee's PF contribution is 12% of (basic + DA). The employer also contributes an equal amount to PF. The employee's net salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹28,000
Step 1: Gross = 25,000 + 5,000 (DA) + 1,600 = ₹31,600
Step 2: Employee's PF = 12% × ₹30,000 = ₹3,600
Step 3: Net = ₹31,600 − ₹3,600 = ₹28,000 (the employer's share is an extra cost to the employer, not a deduction from salary)
Common mistake: Also deducting the employer's share gives ₹24,400 (B). ₹31,600 (C) is gross salary. PF on gross salary gives ₹27,808 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Sourcing accounting software — ready-to-use, customised and tailor-made
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about accounting software:
(A) Ready-to-use software is relatively cheap and easy to install.
(B) Tailor-made software is expensive to develop.
(C) Customised software is a standard package modified to suit the user's needs.
(D) Ready-to-use software offers the greatest flexibility to change its features.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Ready-to-use packages are low-cost and quick to set up (A). Tailor-made software is built from scratch and is costly (B). Customised software adapts a standard package (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — ready-to-use software has the LEAST flexibility; tailor-made software is the most flexible. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Cost and flexibility rise together: ready-to-use → customised → tailor-made.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — useful features
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Feature)
(A) Freeze Panes
(B) Conditional Formatting
(C) Filter
(D) Protect Sheet

List-II (Use in an accounting sheet)
(I) Keeps the heading row visible while scrolling through a long ledger
(II) Highlights overdue debtors in red automatically
(III) Shows only the rows for a selected customer
(IV) Prevents formulas in a payroll sheet from being changed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Freeze Panes locks rows or columns in view (I).
(B) Conditional Formatting formats cells that meet a rule (II).
(C) Filter displays only matching rows (III).
(D) Protect Sheet locks cells against editing (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Freeze Panes and Conditional Formatting; (B) swaps Conditional Formatting and Filter; (C) swaps Freeze Panes and Protect Sheet.
Key point: View, highlight, select, protect.
